subtype: Approach: buying in a rush from fear of rising prices [Pitfall]
passage:
'Ten more people are coming to see it tomorrow,' said Deepak. 'The agent says prices will jump next month.'
'It looks fine,' said Kunal, scrolling through the photos. 'Fine is fine, right?'
'Then let's pay the booking amount tonight.'
They did.
Six weeks later, Kunal was reading a notice from the housing society. 'There's a monthly maintenance charge nobody mentioned. And a separate lift fund.'
'And I timed the route to the office this morning,' Deepak said, rubbing both eyes. 'Ninety minutes in traffic. We never even tried the commute.'
'We were so scared of missing the chance.'
'I know.'
Neither spoke for a while. The booking amount was not coming back.

qa.q: What did Deepak and Kunal find out after paying the booking amount?
qa.a: They found a monthly maintenance charge, a separate lift fund, and a ninety-minute commute to the office.

qa.q: What were Deepak and Kunal afraid of when they booked so quickly, and how can you tell?
qa.a: They were afraid of missing the chance, as Kunal says, because they had heard prices would jump next month.

qa.q: What could they have done differently before paying?
qa.a: They could have asked about every monthly cost and tried the commute first, since fear of rising prices does not remove the need to check.

qa.q: How might the agent's message about prices have felt to the couple later?
qa.a: It may now seem like pressure that pushed them past checking, which is why the couple went quiet.

grounding: Deepak and Kunal rush to book the first flat that seems fine and later meet hidden costs and a longer commute.

subtype: Approach: buying in a rush from fear of rising prices [Pitfall]
passage:
Everyone that year kept saying the same thing: "Prices will jump after the metro opens. Buy now or never."
Sachin and I heard it at work, from relatives, from the man selling sweet corn outside our building in Noida. So when we saw the first flat that seemed fine, a two-bedroom on the eighth floor, we paid the booking amount that same afternoon. It felt brave. It felt grown-up.
We never asked about maintenance. After we moved in, the society bill arrived: much more than we'd guessed, plus a charge for the clubhouse we'd never use.
And the commute. We'd visited on a Sunday. On a Monday morning, the drive to Sachin's office took almost two hours.
I still like the flat. But every month, when the maintenance bill comes, I remember how scared we were of missing out, and how little we actually checked.
— Gurleen

qa.q: What floor was the flat on?
Why did Gurleen and Sachin feel they had to pay the booking amount that afternoon?
qa.a: They were afraid of missing out as everyone warned prices would jump, and the rush made them feel brave even though they checked very little.

qa.q: What else could Gurleen and Sachin have done before paying the booking amount?
qa.a: They could have asked about maintenance charges, tried the commute on a weekday morning, and had the papers checked by a lawyer.

qa.q: How might Sachin be affected by the flat they chose?
qa.a: Sachin faces a drive of almost two hours on Monday mornings, which may leave Sachin tired and frustrated.

grounding: It shows a couple paying a booking amount on the first acceptable flat for fear of rising prices, then finding hidden maintenance costs and a long commute.

subtype: Approach: buying in a rush from fear of rising prices [Pitfall]
passage:
Workplace wellbeing officer's note — conversation with Jagdish, accounts team, Chennai office. Written by Keerthana.

Jagdish asked to talk because he'd been late four times this month and wanted to explain before his manager raised it.
He and his wife bought a flat in March. A relative had warned that prices near the new highway would double within a year, so they paid the booking amount the day they saw it. He said they felt they had no time to think.
After moving in, they found the maintenance charges were far higher than the builder had mentioned, and there was a separate fee for a generator. The bus to our office takes nearly two hours in the morning traffic; they had only visited on a holiday.
He looked tired and embarrassed. "We were so scared of missing out that we didn't ask anything."
What I did next: I shared information on our flexible-timing policy and suggested he speak to his manager openly.

qa.q: How many times had Jagdish been late that month?
How did Jagdish seem to feel during the conversation?
qa.a: He seemed tired and embarrassed, regretting that fear of missing out had stopped them from asking questions.

qa.q: What else could Jagdish and his wife have done before paying the booking amount?
qa.a: They could have asked the builder in writing about all charges, tried the commute on a working day, and taken time to compare options.

qa.q: How is the note-writer affected by what Jagdish shared?
qa.a: The note-writer understands the reason for the lateness and can point Jagdish to flexible timing, rather than seeing it only as a discipline problem.

grounding: It shows a couple booking the first acceptable flat for fear of rising prices, then discovering hidden maintenance costs and a longer commute.
